conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for making time for this visit. I’m Dr. Lee, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My role is simply to check in on how you’re adjusting to life after having your baby, and to be sure you feel supported.

I’ll be using a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale** (EPDS). It’s just ten questions about how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days, and it helps us pick up on signs of depression, anxiety, or distress that sometimes show up during the postpartum months. Everything you share is confidential, and there are no right or wrong answers—only what’s true for you.

We’ll go through the questions conversationally; you can answer in your own words, and we’ll take it at your pace. If any question feels difficult, we can pause. At the end we’ll talk together about what the results mean and what supports might help.

Ready to begin?

**Question 1:** Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt hard to do?

I’ve noticed it’s gotten harder. I used to laugh easily, but lately—unless something’s really hilarious—I mostly feel flat. I’ll smile for the baby or when my husband tries to cheer me up, but it feels forced rather than natural.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I’m sorry… I don’t think that fits for me. Most of the time I can’t find the funny side at all. Even when my husband makes a joke he knows I’d normally love, it just feels flat or I have to fake a chuckle. The only smiles I manage easily are for the baby, and even those feel kind of heavy.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but this week nothing feels worth looking forward to. I still do them because I know I “should,” but the spark isn’t there. It’s like I’m just going through the motions.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s something I ate or that I’m not soothing him right. When I couldn’t get him to latch yesterday, I sat there crying, telling myself I’m already failing him. Even little stuff—like spilling a bottle—turns into “I’m a terrible mom.” I know in my head it’s not all my fault, but the guilty thoughts just jump in.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes, pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly my heart’s racing, wondering if he’s breathing okay, if the house is too cold, if the diaper’s too tight—things that don’t really need checking. It’s like my mind keeps spinning “what-ifs” even when everything looks fine. I can sometimes talk myself down, but the worry just pops back up a little later.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah, it’s happened a few times this week. Out of nowhere I’ll get this rush—my chest feels tight, I can’t catch my breath, and I’m convinced something awful is about to happen, even though nothing’s going on. The first night home from the hospital I woke up dripping sweat, heart pounding, sure the baby had stopped breathing. I checked him, he was fine, but it took almost an hour before I stopped shaking.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes. Most days feel like I’m drowning in small tasks—nursing, changing, trying to sleep, rinse and repeat—and it still seems like too much. I’ll start one thing, remember three others, then the baby cries and everything piles up. I manage to get through it, but I’m running on empty and feel like I’m barely treading water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah, that’s been happening. A few nights this week I lie down exhausted, but my brain won’t shut off—kept replaying everything I might be doing wrong or imagining worst-case scenarios about the baby. I’ll toss and turn for an hour or two, finally drift off, then wake up with my heart racing. Even when the baby’s sleeping a longer stretch, I’m still up two or three times because the anxious thoughts jerk me awake.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day. I wake up feeling heavy, like there’s this gray cloud hanging over everything. Little moments with the baby will bring a quick smile, but then the sadness settles right back in. I find myself tearing up over nothing—just looking out the window or folding onesies—and thinking, “Is this really my life now?” I keep waiting for the old me to show up, but she hasn’t.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened a couple of times this week. Once was after I finally got him down for a nap and the dog barked and woke him—I just sat on the floor and sobbed. Another night I was washing bottles, felt this wave of “I can’t do this,” and the tears started and wouldn’t stop for maybe twenty minutes. It’s not all-day crying, but when it hits, it feels really overwhelming.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

It… it has crossed my mind. Just brief flashes—like when I’m rocking the baby at 3 a.m. and feel so tired and useless, I’ll think, “What if I just disappeared?” or picture myself not waking up. There’s no plan, no real urge to act on it, but the thought pops in maybe once or twice, and then I feel guilty for even letting it show up.

Hearing how hard these early weeks have been for you shows real strength. From the constant self-blame when the baby fusses to the sudden waves of panic that leave you shaking, your descriptions reveal a heavy weight of sadness, worry, and exhaustion that goes far beyond typical new-mom stress. You're doing your best to meet your baby's needs while feeling disconnected from joy, and those passing thoughts of disappearing show how overwhelmed you feel right now.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports complete inability to experience humor, needing to fake laughter, matching "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, describing activities as joyless and mechanical, aligning with "Hardly at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intense self-blame for multiple everyday incidents, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive daily anxiety with intrusive "what-ifs" about the baby that repeatedly return after being talked down, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple sudden panic episodes with physical symptoms and catastrophic fears, matching "Yes, quite a lot".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent overwhelm and difficulty coping daily, aligning with 'sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly sleep disruption tied to unhappiness/anxious rumination, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily sadness with pervasive tearfulness and hopelessness, matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple discrete crying episodes triggered by frustration/helplessness, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 26 places you well above the 14-point cutoff that signals probable major <med>postpartum depression</med> requiring immediate evaluation. You endorsed the two core mood items (Q1, Q2) at maximum severity, describing complete loss of humor and anticipatory pleasure, which aligns with <med>DSM-5 criterion A1</med>. Daily <sym>guilt</sym>, <sym>tearfulness</sym>, and <sym>feelings of inadequacy</sym> meet <med>criterion A2</med>; <sym>sleep disruption</sym> driven by anxious rumination meets <med>criterion A4</med>; and recurrent <sym>panic episodes</sym> and <sym>psychomotor agitation</sm> satisfy <med>criterion A5</med>. Passive thoughts of <quote>not waking up</quote> on Q10, though without plan or intent, still indicate safety concern per EPDS guidelines. Taken together, symptoms cluster supports likely <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Seek urgent same-week appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> to review these results and discuss treatment options including <med>antidepressant medication</med> and <med>therapy</med>.
2. Call the Postpartum Support International helpline 1-800-944-4773 or text 800-944-4773 for 24/7 support and local provider referrals.
3. Arrange practical help-ask a trusted friend or relative to stay overnight or handle household tasks so you can aim for four-hour stretches of sleep; adequate rest is a key part of recovery.
4. Practice 5-minute <med>breathing exercises</med> or guided mindfulness during baby's naps to reduce <sym>physiological arousal</sym> from panic.
5. Schedule a follow-up screen in two weeks to monitor symptom change after intervention is started.
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Symptoms endorsed  
- Persistent anhedonia, pervasive sadness, tearfulness  
- Marked guilt / self-blame regarding infant care  
- Recurrent intrusive worries, nocturnal panic, autonomic arousal  
- Sleep disruption secondary to rumination  
- Subjective sense of being overwhelmed, “drowning”  
- Passive self-harm ideation without intent or plan  

Pattern  
All EPDS-equivalent items positive; distress evident across mood, anxiety, and coping domains.

Risk factors  
- Daily low mood with crying spells  
- Loss of pleasure in previously enjoyed activities  
- Insomnia not solely infant-driven  
- Heightened anxiety/panic episodes  
- Excessive guilt / feelings of maternal inadequacy  
- Passive suicidal thoughts (no plan, means, or intent)

Screening impression  
High likelihood of major postpartum depressive and anxiety symptoms; safety concern re: passive suicidal ideation. Recommend immediate comprehensive psychiatric evaluation, formal assessment tool scoring, and safety planning.
